name: Causal Loop Diagrams
subject: quantum-computing
subjectTitle: A Skeptic's Guide to Quantum Computing

lesson.title: Drawing the Machine Behind the Headlines
lesson.summary: A causal loop diagram is a simple map of cause and effect, arrows carrying plus or minus signs between variables, that reveals the feedback structure driving a system instead of just its latest headline.
lesson.body:
Systems thinking, the broader discipline this book keeps returning to, starts from a simple but stubborn insight: most of the outcomes we care about, in quantum computing or anywhere else, are produced not by isolated events but by loops of cause and effect that circle back on themselves. A causal loop diagram, usually abbreviated CLD, is the basic tool for drawing those loops. You write down the variables that matter, things like public excitement, research funding, or qubit count, as short labeled nodes, then draw arrows between the ones that influence each other, and mark each arrow with a plus or a minus.

The plus and minus signs are doing real work, not decoration. An arrow marked plus means that when the variable at its tail goes up, the variable at its head tends to go up too, and when the tail goes down, the head goes down, all else being equal. An arrow marked minus means the two move in opposite directions: more of one produces less of the other. A CLD is different from an ordinary flowchart, which usually shows a one-way sequence of steps with a clear beginning and end. A CLD is built to loop. Trace the arrows around a CLD and you eventually arrive back where you started, and that closed path, not any single arrow, is the actual unit of analysis in systems thinking.

Consider a small CLD relevant to this book. Draw four nodes: impressive research result, media coverage, public and investor excitement, and funding for more research. An impressive result increases media coverage, plus. Media coverage increases public and investor excitement, plus. Excitement increases funding, plus. And funding, given enough time, tends to produce more impressive results to report, plus. Four nodes, four arrows, and the arrows close into a loop. Nothing in that diagram tells you yet whether this loop will spiral upward forever, settle into balance, or collapse. That classification, reinforcing or balancing, is the subject of the next two chapters. What the CLD alone gives you is the shape: a self-referential structure where funding is quietly downstream of its own past success.

This matters because the alternative to drawing the loop is usually to explain outcomes by blaming or crediting individuals: a charismatic executive, an overzealous journalist, a gullible investor. Loop thinking does not deny that individual choices matter, but it insists that individuals are operating inside a structure that rewards certain choices and punishes others, and that structure persists even as the individuals inside it change. Fire the executive but leave the loop intact, and a new executive tends to behave remarkably similarly, because the loop is still pushing on them the same way it pushed on their predecessor.

Throughout the rest of this section, we will build several concrete CLDs specific to quantum computing: the hype cycle, the sunk cost dynamics inside labs and companies that have already spent heavily on one approach, and the international funding competition between governments. Each of those is, underneath the specific vocabulary, just a CLD with a particular set of nodes and signed arrows. Learning to read the diagram is learning to see the machine that produces the headlines, rather than reacting to the headlines one at a time.
